feedback: If a learner puts everything in 'both', ask them to name one thing that would look different walking through a Scottish oakwood versus the Amazon — most clearly the temperature and the particular species (and, as a general tendency, the greater species richness of tropical forests).
If a learner separates rainfall by type, correct gently: high rainfall is the shared defining feature placed in the overlap — it is temperature and species that differ.
A Venn-style layout (shared features in the overlap, distinct species to each side) makes the shared-vs-different structure visible.
activities.intendedInsight: Temperate and tropical rainforests share structure and the rainfall criterion but differ in temperature and species communities — they are not identical.
learnerActions: Sort a set of features and organisms into three groups: 'tropical only', 'temperate only', or 'both'.
Place shared features in 'both': very high rainfall, dense wet canopy, constant humidity.

Place the clearly distinguishing items correctly: hot climate, kapok trees, hyper-diverse multi-layered canopy (tropical); cooler climate, ancient oaks, giant redwoods (temperate). Put tree ferns, orchids, climbing vines (lianas) and moss-draped trees in 'both' or discuss them rather than scoring them: tree ferns grow in many tropical rainforests as well as New Zealand, orchids and vines also grow in some temperate rainforests (e.g. New Zealand, Chile), and moss-draped trees are a feature shared by both types, though thick moss and lichen are especially typical of temperate ones.
After sorting, discuss a broad pattern (not a scored sort item): temperate rainforests usually have fewer tree species than tropical ones — treat this as a general tendency rather than a fixed rule.
Explain each 'both' placement by naming the feature all rainforests share.
activities.title: Sort it: tropical, temperate, or both

feedback: Full response: explains that persistent high rainfall and humidity define a rainforest, names real temperate examples, and distinguishes temperate (cooler, moss/fern-rich, and typically fewer tree species) from tropical, applying the criterion to a new case.

Partial response: accepts temperate rainforests exist but justifies it weakly or assumes they look identical to tropical ones, without naming year-round rainfall as the defining criterion — prompt for the single defining condition.
Gap response: insists rainforests only exist in hot tropical places and rejects the Scottish/Chilean example — return to the map and definition before re-asking.
activities.intendedInsight: Applying the rainfall criterion lets you judge new or borderline cases: a cool wet coast can be rainforest, while a hot place with a long dry season is usually classed as dry forest or savanna rather than rainforest.
learnerActions: Respond to the prompt: 'Someone says there is real rainforest in cool, rainy places like western Scotland and Wales, and along the coast of Canada and Chile — nowhere near the Equator. Could that be true? Tell me WHY.'
Then tackle a trickier case: 'What if a place is hot but has a long dry season every year — would you usually call it a rainforest? Why or why not?'

Write an explanation that names persistent high rainfall and humidity (not heat) as the defining criterion, names at least two real temperate examples, and states one way a temperate rainforest differs from a tropical one.

Discuss why temperate rainforests are rare worldwide, why they are often found on coasts facing wet winds from the ocean (western coasts in most of these examples), and why places like Britain now have only small fragments left.
activities.title: Judge a borderline case and say why
